name: Frozen dessert
standfirst: All of these are a sweetened liquid taken below freezing. What separates them is whether there is dairy in it, whether an egg was cooked into it first, whether it moves while it freezes — and how much air ends up trapped inside.
root: A sweetened liquid · taken below freezing

dishes.name: Ice cream (Philadelphia style)
dishes.note: The uncooked one — cream, sugar and flavour go into the machine as they are. Everything with a custard below it has added a step before the cold.

dishes.name: French ice cream
dishes.note: Crème anglaise, chilled and then churned. One column apart from Philadelphia style and a different dessert in the mouth: yolk fat coats the tongue where cream fat only fills it.

dishes.name: Frozen custard
dishes.note: French ice cream with the air taken out and the hardening step skipped. American law will only let you call it custard at 1.4 percent egg yolk solids or more.

dishes.name: Soft serve
dishes.note: Sits beside frozen custard in the same machine and makes the opposite choice: less fat and much more air. Served at about −4°C rather than −18°C, which is why it curls.

dishes.name: Gelato
dishes.note: Less fat than ice cream and much less air, served warm enough to be soft. Less fat means less coating on the tongue, so the flavour arrives faster and leaves sooner.

dishes.name: Semifreddo
dishes.note: The air goes in before the cold instead of during it. Whipped cream and meringue hold it there, so no machine is needed and it never freezes hard.

dishes.name: Kulfi
dishes.note: An hour of boiling before anything gets cold. There is too little free water left for crystals to grow, so stillness costs nothing — and the long heat leaves it tasting cooked.

dishes.name: Dondurma
dishes.note: Maraş dondurma. Flour from wild orchid tubers and resin from mastic trees make it elastic enough to cut with a knife, and slow enough to melt that it can be sold from an unrefrigerated cart.

dishes.name: Frozen yogurt
dishes.note: The tang is acid from the culture, not anything the freezing did. Strip the fat out and the sourness has nothing to hide behind, which is the whole flavour.

dishes.name: Sorbet
dishes.note: No dairy at all, so the sugar is doing structural work as well as sweetening — too little and it sets like a rock, too much and it never sets.

dishes.name: Sherbet
dishes.note: Sorbet with 1 to 2 percent milkfat stirred in — genuinely sorbet plus one thing. The dairy is there to blunt the ice crystals, not to taste of cream.

dishes.name: Granita
dishes.note: The same syrup as sorbet, left alone and broken up by hand every half hour. Crystals are the point rather than the failure.

dishes.name: Helado de paila

freeze: turned by hand in a copper pan

dishes.note: A copper bowl set on ice and salt and spun by hand with a wooden paddle. Ibarra has done it since 1897, originally with ice carried down from the glacier on Imbabura.

dishes.name: Faloodeh
dishes.note: Shiraz's answer, and one of the oldest in the family: cold starch vermicelli set through a half-frozen syrup, so every spoonful is chewy and icy at the same time.

dishes.name: Halo-halo
dishes.note: The ice itself is bare — everything that makes it a dessert is spooned in afterwards: ube, sweet beans, leche flan, and evaporated milk poured over the top. The name means mix-mix.

dishes.name: Bingsu
dishes.note: Halo-halo's move applied to dairy instead of water: freeze the milk into a block and shave it. You get creaminess without ever churning, in ribbons rather than a scoop.

notes.title: On moving while it freezes
notes.body: This is the largest fork in the family. Movement keeps ice crystals small, and small crystals are what the word creamy actually describes. Leave the mix still and you need another answer to the same problem: accept the crystals and make them the point (granita), trap the air beforehand in whipped cream and meringue (semifreddo), or boil the milk down until there is too little free water for crystals to grow at all (kulfi).

notes.title: On air
notes.body: Air is the invisible ingredient, and the trade has a name — overrun, how much the mix expands in the machine. American ice cream may nearly double in volume so long as a gallon still weighs 4.5 pounds. Gelato takes far less, which is why a small cup of it is surprisingly heavy. Frozen custard takes almost none. Same cream, same sugar, three desserts, and most of the difference is nothing.

notes.title: On giving water a body
notes.body: Frozen sugar-water has nothing holding it together, and four traditions answer that four different ways: egg yolk in France, salep and mastic in Maraş, starch noodles set through the syrup in Shiraz, and in North India no additive at all — just milk boiled down until its own solids do the work. These are siblings solving one problem, not versions of each other.

notes.title: On the word sherbet
notes.body: In American law sherbet is sorbet with 1 to 2 percent milkfat, and it is the only dish here whose lineage is a legal definition. In Britain sherbet is a fizzy sweet powder with nothing to do with any of this. Across much of the rest of the anglophone world it is simply what sorbet is called. Three things, one word — all of them descended from the Arabic sharbat.
